title: Software developer

manager.name: Noor
manager.title: Engineering Manager
manager.persona_note: Noor wants a safe choice, and big names can feel safe. A good recruiter turns those labels into skills you can actually check.

teaser: Noor leads a team of developers and has firm ideas about where the best ones come from.
context: The company handles payments for small businesses and has about 70 people.
The new developer joins a team of five and reports to Noor.
message: Hi! I'm hiring a senior developer for the team that runs our customers' payments. It's an important role, and I want to get it right this time.
The job ad is a wish list from a while ago, so take it with a grain of salt.
Do you have ten minutes to go over what we need?
ad: Computer science degree from a top university
framing: Kickoff calls are often short, and hiring managers have a lot on their plate. Noor will share a few first thoughts about the role. Good questions help you both get it right.
end_early: Sorry, I've got to jump into a meeting. Send me what you've got.

needs.n1: Someone to keep the payment system running as it grows, and fix it when it breaks.
needs.n2: Someone to help the junior developers grow and set standards for the team.
needs.n3: Someone to build a new product from scratch and get it to customers quickly.

beats.label: The timeline
beats.sam: I need a senior developer as soon as possible. Could you send me people from big tech companies by next week?

choices.text: I can move quickly. Before I do, what happened with the last person in this role?
choices.reply: We had a senior developer. It didn't work out, and they left after seven months.
choices.why: Asking about the last hire before agreeing to a timeline is the quickest way to learn what really matters for this search.

choices.text: Should I start with big tech and adjust once we see who's out there?
choices.reply: Yes, speed matters here.
choices.why: It sounds efficient, but you'd be adjusting without a target, and 'big tech' is an assumption you haven't tested yet.

choices.text: Is next week realistic for a senior developer, though?
choices.reply: That's what the last recruiter said.
choices.why: Questioning the deadline before you understand the need turns the conversation into a standoff.

choices.text: What would you want the next person to do differently?
choices.reply: They wrote great code, but wouldn't help when the system broke at night. Our junior developers carried it.
choices.why: An open follow-up turns 'it didn't work out' into the real lesson, which is what you'll screen for.

choices.text: So they just weren't technical enough?
choices.reply: No, they were very technical.
choices.why: A leading question guesses the answer, and here it guessed wrong. An open question gets the real story.

choices.text: Do you think the team supported them properly?
choices.reply: I think we did, yes.
choices.why: It might be worth knowing later, but right now it sounds like blame and puts the manager on the defensive.

beats.label: Education
beats.sam: And ideally they studied computer science at a top university.

choices.text: What would strong skills look like in the work itself, wherever someone studied?
choices.reply: Fair. Someone who thinks about how things can break, and designs for it.
choices.why: Shifting from where someone studied to what they can do gives you a standard you can test, and it keeps strong self-taught developers in the search.

choices.text: Would a degree from any good program work, or does it need to be a specific school?
choices.reply: Any good program would do, I suppose.
choices.why: It loosens the filter a little, but you're still screening on a credential instead of the skills the job needs.

choices.text: Should I focus my search on the top schools, then?
choices.reply: Yes, perfect.
choices.why: Going along with it narrows the search to a credential that tells you very little about how someone will do the job.

beats.label: The must-have
beats.sam: They must know Go. It says so in the ad.

choices.text: Did your strongest developers know Go when they joined?
choices.reply: Honestly, no. Most of them learned it here in a few weeks.
choices.why: Checking a must-have against the people who already do well often shows it's a nice-to-have, which widens your search.

choices.text: Should I put Go experience at the top of the screening list?
choices.reply: Yes, let's do that.
choices.why: It sounds reasonable, but you've narrowed the search on an assumption nobody has tested.

choices.text: So Go is a deal-breaker, then?
choices.reply: Yes, definitely.
choices.why: A yes-or-no question pushed the manager to dig in, and now an untested must-have is locked in.

beats.label: Proof
beats.sam: People from big tech companies just know how to build things properly.

choices.text: What will they need to have done before to be successful here?
choices.reply: Kept a busy system running, including fixing it when it breaks, even at night.
choices.why: Asking what success requires moves the conversation from company names to proof you can check.

choices.text: So big tech experience is the main thing you're looking for?
choices.reply: Pretty much.
choices.why: A closed question invites the manager to confirm the assumption, when what you really want is to test it.

choices.text: Isn't big tech experience a bit overrated for a team your size?
choices.reply: Not by our investors.
choices.why: A flat challenge starts a debate you won't win in a kickoff meeting.

beats.label: The pay
beats.sam: Pay is competitive. Let's not get into numbers yet.

choices.text: So I only bring you people you can actually hire, what range can you approve today?
choices.reply: $140,000 to $160,000 base salary. There's a bit more for the right person, but it's hard.
choices.why: Linking the question to finding the right people makes the number easy to share.

choices.text: I really can't recruit without a number. Would you mind sharing one?
choices.why: It worked, but it cost you some goodwill. A question tied to their goal gets the same answer more smoothly.

choices.text: Is it okay if we sort out pay later in the process?
choices.reply: Sure.
choices.why: Without a range, you can't tell which candidates you can actually afford, and late surprises lose people.

beats.note: Since January 2026, many Ontario employers must include the expected pay or a pay range in public job postings.

beats.label: Office days
beats.sam: We'd like them in the office two days a week. Is that a problem?

choices.text: That sounds reasonable. So I can explain it to candidates, what usually happens on those two days?
choices.reply: Design reviews and planning. It's when our junior developers get the most help.
choices.why: Accepting a reasonable request, then asking what happens on those days, shows curiosity and gives you a real selling point for candidates.

choices.text: Is that flexible for the right person?
choices.reply: Not really. The team works together on those days.
choices.why: It's a fair question, but asked before you understand why those days matter, it can sound like you're already negotiating against the manager.

choices.text: Most developers I talk to want to be fully remote. Could we drop the office days?
choices.reply: No. We've been clear about that.
choices.why: Pushing to change a settled decision, with nothing to back it up, spends goodwill you'll need for the questions that actually change the search.

beats.label: Selling the role
beats.sam: Honestly, any good developer could do this job.

choices.text: What would make a great developer pick this job over their other options?
choices.reply: They'd own the system that moves our customers' money, and decide how it grows.
choices.why: Asking what makes the job attractive tells you what's really different about it, and that's your pitch.

choices.text: Should I focus on strong developers in general, then?
choices.reply: Exactly.
choices.why: It sounds sensible, but you'd miss what makes this job different, which is what attracts the right person.

choices.text: Don't you think the job itself matters to good developers?
choices.reply: I didn't say it didn't.
choices.why: Questioning the manager rarely changes their mind. Asking what makes the job appealing does.

candidates.name: Ari
candidates.job: Senior developer at a payments company
facts: Leads the team that handles problems day or night
Redesigned the system so one failure can't take it down
Helped the system handle 10 times more customers

reason.n1: Keeps a busy payment system running and steps up when it breaks. At $163,000 they're a little over the range, but Noor said there's a bit more for the right person.

view.n1: Ari is worth stretching the budget for.

candidates.name: Harlow
candidates.job: Senior developer at an online bank
facts: Rebuilt a payment service to handle 5 times more traffic
Works alongside an operations team that covers nights

reason.n1: Strong and careful, but an operations team handles problems at night. Noor's last hire didn't help when things broke at night, and that's what this job needs.

view.n1: Harlow would leave the night problems to someone else.

candidates.name: Kendall
candidates.job: Lead developer at a software company
facts: Expert in Go, the language in the ad
Set the team's rules for reviewing code

reason.n1: The Go expertise matches the old ad, but Noor confirmed most of the team learned Go here in weeks. Kendall's strength is growing a team.

view.n1: Kendall's great with people. That's not this job.

candidates.name: Briar
candidates.job: Senior engineer at a famous global tech company
facts: Built features used by millions of people
Computer science degree from a top university
Works on a team of 40 engineers

reason.n1: The most impressive resume, but built on new features inside a huge team. Noor needs someone who keeps a busy system running and fixes it when it breaks.

view.n1: Briar builds the shiny parts. I need someone who keeps the lights on.
